mainTopic: The fetus (עובר) and the mother's שחיטה: whether a foreleg that left the womb stays forbidden, as רב rules, and the גמרא's challenges to him from the משנה and a ברייתא.
overview: The משנה teaches that the mother's שחיטה normally permits the fetus inside her. If the fetus only put out its foreleg and pulled it back, it is still permitted. If it put out its head, it counts as born and needs its own שחיטה. Pieces cut from the fetus inside the womb are permitted, but pieces cut from the mother's own organs stay forbidden. רב adds that the foreleg that came out is itself forbidden, learning from the פסוק of טרפה that meat which leaves its boundary becomes forbidden. The גמרא challenges רב from the משנה's words 'brought it back'. Along the way it shows that the head clause teaches nothing new: בכורות covers a person, and the placenta משנה covers an animal. The גמרא defends רב by saying 'brought it back' teaches a rule about the spot of the cut. It then brings a ברייתא with several cases about a foreleg that came out, and that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A fetus that put out its foreleg versus its head
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a fetus which put out its foreleg and pulled it back is still permitted through the mother's שחיטה. If it put out its head, it counts as born.
steps.simpleTranslation: An animal was having a hard time giving birth. The fetus stuck out its foreleg and then pulled it back in. The fetus may be eaten through the mother's שחיטה. But if it stuck out its head, even if it pulled it back in, it counts as a born animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens the topic of a fetus that partly came out of its mother before she was slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fetus inside the mother is normally permitted by her שחיטה, as if it were one of her limbs. A foreleg coming out does not change the status of the whole fetus. But the head coming out makes the fetus 'born', so it becomes its own animal and needs its own שחיטה.

keyTerms.meaning: having difficulty giving birth
fetus
permitted to be eaten
like a born animal

steps.confusionAlert: 'Permitted' here is about the fetus as a whole. The גמרא will soon say that the foreleg itself, the part that came out, is still forbidden.

phrases.english: MISHNA: An animal that is having difficulty giving birth,
and the fetus put out its foreleg and brought it back in,
it is permitted to be eaten.
If it put out its head,
even though it brought it back in,
it is considered like a born animal.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Foreleg out and back in: the fetus is permitted through the mother. Head out: the fetus counts as born and needs its own שחיטה.

steps.title: Cutting from the fetus versus cutting from the mother
steps.stepSummary: Pieces cut from the fetus inside the womb are permitted. Pieces cut from the mother's spleen or kidneys are forbidden. The משנה gives the general rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone cuts a piece from the fetus inside the mother before she is slaughtered, it may be eaten. If he cuts from her spleen or kidneys, it may not. The rule is: something that is part of her body is forbidden, and something that is not part of her body is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case and then sums it up with a general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A piece cut from the mother's own body while she is alive is meat taken from a living animal, and her later שחיטה cannot fix it. The fetus is not considered her body in this way, so a piece cut from it and left inside her is still permitted when she is slaughtered.

keyTerms.meaning: spleen
kidneys
this is the general rule
her own body (of the mother animal)

steps.whatToRemember: The mother's own organs, cut off before שחיטה, stay forbidden. The fetus is not 'her body', so pieces of it left in the womb are permitted by her שחיטה.

phrases.english: One who cuts from a fetus that is inside her womb,
it is permitted to be eaten.
If he cut from the spleen or from the kidneys,
phrases.notes: These are the mother animal's own organs.

phrases.english: it is forbidden to be eaten.
This is the rule: something that is part of her body is forbidden,
and something that is not part of her body is permitted.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Something cut from the mother's body before שחיטה is forbidden. Something cut from the fetus and left in the womb is permitted by her שחיטה.

steps.title: The limb that came out is itself forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב, adds a limit to the משנה's first ruling: the foreleg that came out is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: but the limb itself is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by narrowing the משנה's first case. The fetus is permitted, but the foreleg that went outside is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said 'permitted', which could sound like the whole fetus, foreleg included. רב splits it: the rest of the fetus is permitted through the mother's שחיטה, but the part that left the womb is forbidden even after it came back in.

keyTerms.meaning: the limb itself
forbidden

steps.whyThisMatters: In practice, when such a fetus is eaten through the mother's שחיטה, the foreleg that came out must be cut away and not eaten.

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
But the limb itself is forbidden.
phrases.notes: This is the foreleg from the משנה, the one that went out and was pulled back in.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב וְאֵבֶר עַצְמוֹ אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the first ruling of the משנה (step 1).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The foreleg that left the womb stays forbidden, even though the rest of the fetus is permitted.

steps.title: Why is the limb forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source and reason behind רב's ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the foreleg should be forbidden. This sets up the next step, where the answer comes from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The limb went back inside before the שחיטה, so you might think it is permitted along with the rest of the fetus. The גמרא wants a source showing that leaving the womb makes it forbidden for good.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for forbidding the limb that came out, even though it went back inside.

steps.title: Meat that leaves its boundary becomes forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns from the פסוק of טרפה that meat which goes outside its proper boundary becomes forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the פסוק says: 'And flesh in the field, a טרפה, you shall not eat.' Once meat goes outside its boundary, it becomes forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק and draws a general rule from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'flesh in the field' are read as meat that went outside the place where it belongs. Meat like that becomes forbidden, like a טרפה. The womb is the fetus's boundary, so a foreleg that left the womb became forbidden and stays forbidden even after it goes back in.

keyTerms.meaning: the verse (פסוק)
a fatally wounded animal; here, a name for forbidden meat
outside its boundary
becomes forbidden

steps.whatToRemember: The rule 'כיון שיצא בשר חוץ למחיצתו נאסר': meat that leaves its boundary becomes forbidden. For a fetus, the boundary is the womb.

phrases.english: Because the verse says:
"And flesh in the field, a tereifa, you shall not eat"
once the flesh has gone out
outside its boundary, it becomes forbidden.
phrases.notes: 'In the field' is read as outside the place the meat belongs. For the fetus, that place is the womb.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר קְרָא וּבָשָׂר בַּשָּׂדֶה טְרֵפָה לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'ובשר בשדה טרפה' teaches that meat which leaves its boundary becomes forbidden, so the foreleg that left the womb is forbidden.

steps.title: The משנה seems to permit the foreleg too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה, which says the fetus is permitted, and suggests this includes the foreleg. That would contradict רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if an animal has trouble giving birth, and the fetus puts out its foreleg and pulls it back, it is permitted to eat. Isn't the משנה talking about the limb too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling by pointing to the משנה, which seems to say the whole fetus, foreleg included, is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said the foreleg that came out is forbidden. The משנה says 'permitted' without any limit. If 'permitted' covers the foreleg, the משנה argues against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Having difficulty giving birth
Fetus
Limb, here the foreleg that came out
Is it not? (introduces an assumed reading used to challenge)

phrases.english: We learned: An animal having difficulty giving birth,
and the fetus put out its foreleg and brought it back,
it is permitted to eat.
Is it not referring to the limb as well?
phrases.notes: In other words, the word 'permitted' would cover the foreleg too, and that goes against רב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's ruling (Step 3) using the משנה (Step 1).
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the foreleg which came out is forbidden.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's 'permitted' seems to include the foreleg itself, which contradicts רב.

steps.title: The משנה permits only the rest of the fetus
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה's 'permitted' refers to the fetus, not the foreleg.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it refers to the fetus.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב: the משנה permits the body of the fetus, but not the foreleg that went out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer narrows the משנה. 'Permitted' is about the rest of the fetus, so the foreleg can still be forbidden, just as רב said. The two sources no longer clash.

keyTerms.meaning: No, the answer rejects the assumption

phrases.english: No, it refers to the fetus.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה permits the foreleg as well.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה permits only the rest of the fetus; the foreleg is forbidden, as רב said.

steps.title: Then why mention that it brought the foreleg back?
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה is only about the rest of the fetus, the detail 'brought it back' seems pointless.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it refers to the fetus, why specifically say it brought it back? Even if it did not bring it back, the fetus would also be permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave: if only the body of the fetus is permitted, pulling the foreleg back should make no difference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the new reading, the rest of the fetus is permitted whether or not the foreleg returned. So the משנה's words 'and brought it back' look unnecessary. The גמרא asks why the משנה included them.

keyTerms.meaning: Why specifically this case? (asks why a detail was mentioned)
Brought it back inside

phrases.english: If it refers to the fetus,
why specifically 'brought it back'?
Even if it did not bring it back, it is also permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 7 from the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the משנה refers only to the rest of the fetus.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If so, the detail 'brought it back' changes nothing and should not have been written.

steps.title: The wording matches the later clause about the head
steps.stepSummary: The rule really applies even without bringing it back, but the משנה said 'brought it back' to match the wording of its next clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true even if it did not bring it back. But since the משנה wanted to teach in the later clause, 'if it put out its head, even though it brought it back, it is like a born animal,' it also said 'brought it back' in the first clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits the detail is not needed for the law, and explains that the משנה used it so both clauses would be worded the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the head case, 'brought it back' really matters: even then it counts as born. The משנה reused the same words in the foreleg case for style. So the reading from Step 7 holds.

keyTerms.meaning: The same law applies
Since, because of (the wording of another clause)
The later clause of a משנה
The first clause of a משנה
Like a born animal; needs its own שחיטה

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think 'brought it back' is a condition for the fetus being permitted. It is only there to match the wording of the head clause.

phrases.english: If it put out its head, even though it brought it back,
it is like a born animal,

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הַדִּין אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא הֶחְזִירוֹ

steps.terutzMaskana: It is not needed for the law; it was written to match the head clause, where it does matter.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה permits the rest of the fetus whether or not the foreleg returned; the foreleg itself is forbidden, as רב said.

steps.title: The head clause seems already taught in בכורות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the head clause adds, since a משנה in בכורות already shows that a head coming out counts as birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the later clause, what does it teach us? That once the head came out, it counts as a birth? We already learned: Who is a firstborn for inheritance but not a firstborn for the כהנים? One who came after a miscarried fetus, even if its head came out alive, or after a nine-month baby whose head came out dead.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the משנה's later clause and asks why it is needed, quoting another משנה that seems to teach the same idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה's head clause teaches that a head coming out counts as birth. The גמרא brings the משנה about בכור לנחלה, and in the next step it will draw that same idea from it. If so, our clause looks repetitive.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it teaching us? (asks what a statement adds)
Firstborn for receiving a double inheritance from the father
Firstborn who must be redeemed by giving money to a כהן
Miscarried fetuses that could not live
A full-term, nine-month baby

phrases.english: And the later clause, what does it teach us?

phrases.aramaic: דְּכֵיוָן דְּיָצָא רֹאשׁוֹ הָוְיָא לַהּ לֵידָה?
phrases.english: That once its head came out, it counts as a birth?
We already learned: Who is a firstborn for inheritance
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in בכורות 46a.

phrases.english: but not a firstborn for the כהנים?
One who came after miscarried fetuses,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיָּצָא רֹאשׁוֹ חַי,
phrases.english: even if its head came out alive,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בֶּן תִּשְׁעָה שֶׁיָּצָא רֹאשׁוֹ מֵת.
phrases.english: or a nine-month baby whose head came out dead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having explained the first clause, the גמרא now questions the need for the later clause it just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's clause that a fetus whose head came out is like a born animal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same rule can already be learned from the משנה in בכורות, so this clause seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Drawing the head rule from the בכורות משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows how the בכורות משנה teaches that a head coming out alive counts as birth, finishing the challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is that its head came out dead. But if its head came out alive, the one born after it would not be a firstborn even for inheritance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes its challenge by reading a hidden rule out of the בכורות משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The next son is a בכור לנחלה only because the full-term baby's head came out dead. If the head came out alive, that already counts as a birth, so the next son is not the first. So 'a head coming out counts as birth' is already known, and our clause seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is (sets up an inference from a detail)
But in the opposite case (introduces the inferred rule)

phrases.english: The reason is that its head came out dead,
but if its head came out alive,

phrases.aramaic: הַבָּא אַחֲרָיו בְּכוֹר לְנַחֲלָה נָמֵי לָא הָוֵי.
phrases.english: the one who comes after it would not be a firstborn even for inheritance.

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּרֹאשׁוֹ מֵת, הָא רֹאשׁוֹ חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge of Step 10 by drawing the rule out of the בכורות משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That a head coming out alive counts as a birth is already known, so our משנה's head clause seems unnecessary.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בכורות about בכור לנחלה, read through what its words imply.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next step, where the גמרא must explain what our משנה's head clause adds.

steps.title: Maybe our משנה teaches the rule for animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the בכורות משנה taught the head rule for a person, while our משנה teaches it for an animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: that משנה taught us about a person, and this משנה teaches us about an animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a possible way to save our משנה's head clause from the challenge of Step 10. It says the two משניות cover two different cases: people and animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge was that the בכורות משנה already teaches that a head coming out counts as birth. The answer is that the בכורות משנה is about a human birth, so our משנה is still needed to teach the same rule for animals.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say: introduces a possible answer that the גמרא will test
It taught us
A person / an animal

phrases.english: And if you would say: it taught us about a person,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the משנה in בכורות from the last two steps, which deals with a human birth.

phrases.english: and this one teaches us about an animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a defense against the redundancy challenge of Steps 10-11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: person in one משנה, animal in the other
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The head clause in our משנה is pointless because בכורות already teaches it.
steps.terutzMaskana: If this suggestion held, each משנה would cover a different subject (person vs. animal), so neither would repeat the other. Step 14 rejects it, because the placenta משנה already teaches the rule for animals.

steps.title: Why a person and an animal each need their own source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the rule could not be learned from a person to an animal, or from an animal to a person.
steps.simpleTranslation: For a person cannot be learned from an animal, since an animal has no hidden entryway. And an animal cannot be learned from a person, since a person's face is important.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the suggestion of Step 12 by showing that both teachings are needed. Each case has something special that keeps us from learning one from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal has no פרוזדור, so its birth is seen at once. That might be different from a woman, where the opening is hidden. A person's face is especially important, so maybe the head counts as birth only for a person. Because of these differences, we would need one source for each.

keyTerms.meaning: Learns, derives one case from another
An entryway; here, the hidden opening of the womb in a woman
The form of the face
Important, significant

phrases.english: For a person cannot be learned from an animal,
since an animal has no hidden entryway,
phrases.notes: In a woman the birth opening is hidden, but an animal's birth is seen right away.

phrases.english: and an animal cannot be learned from a person,
since the form of his face is important.
phrases.notes: 'His' means the person's. Because a human face matters so much, maybe only a person's head counts as birth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 12 by showing why separate teachings are needed for a person and an animal.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that our משנה is needed to teach the head rule for animals
steps.raayaSupportSource: Logical differences: an animal has no פרוזדור, and a person's face is especially important

steps.title: The placenta משנה already teaches the rule for animals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion, because a משנה about a placenta already shows that the head rule applies to animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: This too we have already learned: a placenta that partly came out is forbidden to eat. Just as it is a sign of a baby in a woman, so it is a sign of a baby in an animal!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the answer from Steps 12-13. Even for animals, another משנה already teaches the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If part of a placenta came out, the fetus's head might have been inside that part. The משנה forbids it because a head coming out would count as a birth. So the head rule for animals is already known, and our משנה's head clause again seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: This too we have already learned: shows that a point is already taught elsewhere
Placenta, the sac that holds the fetus
Forbidden to eat
A sign that there is a baby (fetus)

steps.confusionAlert: The placenta משנה never says the word 'head.' The proof comes from its reason: part of the placenta may hold the head, and a head coming out counts as birth.

phrases.english: This too we have learned:
A placenta, part of which came out,
phrases.notes: This is a משנה later in חולין (77a), about an animal before it was slaughtered.

phrases.english: is forbidden to eat,
just as it is a sign of a baby in a woman,
so it is a sign of a baby in an animal!
phrases.notes: The part that came out may have held the head, so the fetus counts as born and the mother's שחיטה does not permit it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the person/animal split by showing the animal case is also already taught.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole suggestion that our משנה's head clause is needed for animals
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The placenta משנה already teaches that a head coming out counts as birth for an animal, so the clause is still extra.
steps.whatToRemember: Our משנה's head clause teaches nothing new: בכורות covers a person, and the placenta משנה covers an animal.

steps.title: Setting up the renewed challenge against רב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to argue that 'brought it back' in the first clause must be meant exactly, against רב's reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, if you say that 'brought it back' in the first clause is meant exactly, then the later clause was taught only to match the first clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It uses the fact that the head clause adds nothing to restart its challenge against רב, and the rest of the argument continues next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'brought it back' in the first clause is meant exactly, the first clause teaches something new: a foreleg that was brought back is permitted. Then the later clause can be there only to match the style of the first, and that is fine. This turns Step 9 around. There, רב's side said the first clause copied the later one. Now we have learned the later clause teaches nothing, so it must be the one that copies.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it makes sense: opens the 'this works' half of an argument

The first clause / the later clause of a משנה

steps.whyThisMatters: This is where the side question about the head clause pays off. It becomes a new attack on רב's view that a foreleg that was brought back is still forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא הֶחְזִירוֹ דְּרֵישָׁא דַּוְקָא

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the later clause teaches nothing new, it cannot be the clause the first one copies. The first clause must be exact, and the later clause copies it.

steps.title: Why mention 'brought it back' at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא completes its challenge: if neither clause of the משנה is exact, the words 'brought it back' would be pointless.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if you say that neither the first clause nor the latter clause is meant exactly, why does the משנה need to teach 'brought it back' at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge it started in the last step. It argues that the משנה's words 'brought it back' must teach something, so the first clause must be exact, and that goes against רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The latter clause about the head is already taught elsewhere: בכורות covers a person and the placenta משנה covers an animal, so it adds nothing new. If the first clause is also not exact, because it is only about the rest of the fetus, then 'brought it back' teaches nothing at all. So the first clause must mean that the foreleg itself is permitted only when it was brought back, which contradicts רב, who forbids the foreleg even if it went back in.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of the משנה (here, the foreleg case)
The latter clause of the משנה (here, the head case)
Exactly, precisely; the wording is meant to teach something
Why does it need to teach it?

phrases.notes: The latter clause is about the head. We already know that rule from other משניות: בכורות for a person, and the placenta משנה for an animal.

steps.kashyaTarget: רב's reading that the משנה's 'permitted' refers only to the rest of the fetus, not the foreleg
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If neither clause is exact, the words 'brought it back' are useless. The משנה does not waste words, so the first clause must be exact, and the foreleg itself is permitted when brought back.

steps.title: The words teach about the spot of the cut
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה really is about the rest of the fetus, and 'brought it back' teaches a rule about the spot where the leg would be cut.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really the משנה is talking about the fetus, and it is like what רב נחמן בר יצחק said: it is needed only for the place of the cut. Here too, it is needed only for the place of the cut.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. It says 'brought it back' does teach something new, but about the spot of the cut, not about permitting the foreleg itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה still means the rest of the fetus is permitted, just as רב says. The words 'brought it back' teach that if the leg was not brought back, even the spot on the body where the leg meets the inside is forbidden. This borrows the idea of רב נחמן בר יצחק, who explained a ברייתא the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually; the original reading stands
It was needed only for...
The spot of the cut, where the limb meets the body at the edge of the womb
Here too; the same explanation works in this case

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not say the foreleg is permitted. רב's view stays: the foreleg itself is forbidden. The extra words only teach about the spot of the cut.

and it is like what Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:

steps.title: A ברייתא about an animal having trouble giving birth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with three cases about a fetus's foreleg, to set up a new challenge against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: An animal was having trouble giving birth. If the fetus put out its foreleg and brought it back, and afterward the mother was slaughtered, it is permitted to eat. If the mother was slaughtered and afterward the leg was brought back, it is forbidden to eat. If the fetus put out its foreleg and someone cut it off, and afterward the mother was slaughtered, the part outside is impure and forbidden, and the part inside is pure and permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to open a new challenge against רב. It is setting up the next move, where it will use this ברייתא to question רב's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case says the fetus is permitted when the leg was returned before the mother was slaughtered, which sounds like even the leg is permitted, against רב. The timing matters: returning the leg after the slaughter does not help. The third case shows a leg left outside and cut off is forbidden, while what was inside is permitted through the mother's slaughter.

keyTerms.meaning: Having a hard time giving birth
Brought it back inside
Permitted to eat
The part that was outside the womb
The part that was inside the womb

steps.whyThisMatters: The order of events, returning the leg before or after the mother's slaughter, decides whether the fetus is permitted. This sets up a strong test of רב's view.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
An animal that was having trouble giving birth,
the fetus put out its foreleg and brought it back,
and afterward one slaughtered its mother:
it is permitted to eat.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁחַט אֶת אִמּוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ הֶחְזִירָהּ –

it is forbidden to eat.
If it put out its foreleg and one cut it off,
and afterward one slaughtered its mother:
what was outside is impure and forbidden,
and what was inside is pure and permitted.

steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a foreleg that came out is forbidden even if brought back
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says 'permitted to eat' when the leg was returned before the slaughter, which seems to include the leg itself.

steps.title: The case where the mother is slaughtered before the leg is cut
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with a case where the mother is slaughtered first and the leg that was outside is cut off only afterward.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone slaughtered the mother first, and only afterward cut off the leg that was sticking out...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps reading the ברייתא it started in Step 18. This line only sets up the next case, and the ruling comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this ברייתא, the order of events matters: was the leg cut before or after the mother's שחיטה? Here the שחיטה happens first, while the leg is still sticking outside, and the cutting comes later. The ברייתא's ruling on this case will be used to test רב's position.

keyTerms.meaning: He slaughtered (did a kosher שחיטה)
Its mother, meaning the animal carrying the fetus
He cut it off, meaning the leg that was sticking out
And afterward. It shows the order of the two actions.

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two orders apart. The case before this one has the leg cut first. In this case the mother is slaughtered first. The ruling may be different because the order is different.
